texts: Learn why auto-generated Claude.md files hurt your coding agents and what to use instead for better performance and lower costs.
If you're using Claude Code or any coding agent, there's an
command that promises to create a
file with documentation about your codebase.
Never run it. If you find one that was auto-generated, delete it.
The file it creates will burn tokens, distract the agent, and go out of date faster than a pear on a hot day.
: unnecessary context files make tasks harder, not easier.

A common piece of advice: if the agent does something you don't like, put a rule in
Maybe it uses npm instead of pnpm. Maybe it reaches for a React pattern you hate. So you add a line.
. Every instruction applies to every session: frontend, backend, docs, database, all of it.
That React rule is useful for frontend sessions. But the next session might be purely backend work where it's completely irrelevant. The session after that might be documentation.
Every line you add has a cost that compounds across every session, whether it's relevant or not.
Init commands tend to generate the same categories of content. All of it is problematic.
Init loves dumping every script from
into the file. These are trivially discoverable. The agent can just read

Framework names, rendering modes, compiler settings. The agent can discover all of this from config files and imports. A
file already tells it you're using React Router. An
import tells it you're using Effect.

How specific features work, what patterns to use where. Not only is this discoverable from the code, it's only relevant to a fraction of sessions. Most tasks won't touch most patterns.
The throughline: everything init generates is either trivially discoverable from source or will go stale. Your file system
the documentation. If you structure it well, the agent gets an accurate picture of your architecture from the source of truth, not from a rotting summary.
Every modern coding agent has an explore phase. Before making changes, it reads files, searches the codebase, and builds up context just-in-time for the task at hand.

because it only loads what's relevant, and it always reflects the current state of the code.
